*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=6$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
S={ {{field-1}}\,:\,n\in {{field-2}} }
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,3,\,6,\,12,\,24,\,48,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =2 \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =\frac{12}{6} \\  & =\frac{24}{12} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=6,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =6\cdot {2}^{n-1} \\  & =6\cdot {2}^{n}\cdot {2}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{6}{2}\cdot {2}^{n} \\  & =3\cdot {2}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S={3\cdot {2}^{n}\,:\,n\in Z}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198873 :question/id #uuid "d9cd56d9-afeb-5bee-b832-904b834a28b7" :question/math-academy-id "q-183783"} {:db/id 17592186287862 :question/id #uuid $$
S={x\in {{field-1}}\,:\,{{field-2}}\le x\le {{field-3}}}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The set $S$ contains all natural numbers between $5$ and $50$ (including $5$ and $50$).

Therefore, the set can be written as

$$
S={x\in N\,:\,5\le x\le 50}.
$$

**Note**: This definition is not unique. For example:

- We can write $x\in Z.$ This gives

$$
S={x\in Z\,:\,5\le x\le 50}.
$$

- We can write $4<x<51.$ This gives

$$
S={x\in N\,:\,4<x<51},
$$

or, writing $x\in Z$ as before, we have

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186199425 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199577 :tutorial/content "As previously seen, we can define sets using so-called *constructive definitions* of the form

$$
\big\{ {\color{blue}\textrm{rule}} \: : \: {\color{blue}\textrm{base set}} \big\}
$$

 

where the ${\color{blue}\textrm{rule}}$ is an expression (or formula) that depends on a variable that *constructs* elements of our set when the variable runs over some ${\color{blue}\textrm{base set}}.$ 

For example, the set $A,$ given by

$$
A = \big\{ 2n+1\, : \, n\in\mathbb N_0 \big \}
$$

is defined constructively and contains all positive odd numbers:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={2n+1\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}} \\  & ={2(0)+1,\,2(1)+1,\,2(2)+1,\,2(3)+1,\,…} \\  & ={1,3,5,7,…}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Sometimes, it's helpful to write a set using a constructive definition. For example, how might we express the following set constructively?

$$
B = \big\{ 4, 7, 10, 13, \ldots \big\}
$$

First, notice that the elements of our set 

$$
4,\quad 7,\quad 10,\quad 13,\quad \ldots
$$

form an arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=3{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =3 \\  & =7-4 \\  & =10-7 \\  & =13-10 \\  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term $a_n$ of our sequence for $n\in\mathbb N$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\cdot d \\  & =4+(n-1)\cdot 3 \\  & =4+3n-3 \\  & =3n+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set constructively as follows:

$$
B = \big\{ 3n+1 \: : \: n \in \mathbb{N} \big\}
$$

The expression $3n+1$ generates the elements of our set when $n$ runs over $\mathbb{N}.$ 

Note the following:

- A bar "$\mid$" is just as acceptable as a colon to separate the rule from the base set. So, we could also express our set as follows:

$$
B=\big\{ 3n+1 \: \mid \: n \in \mathbb{N} \big\}
$$

- The constructive definition of a given set is typically not unique. For example, we could also define $B$ as follows:

$$
B=\big\{ 3n+4 \: :\: n \in \mathbb{N}_0 \big\}
$$

Notice that we used $\mathbb N_0$ as the base set.

This definition does indeed generate all elements of $B{:}$

17592186199577 :tutorial/content "As previously seen, we can define sets using so-called *constructive definitions* of the form

$$
\big\{ {\color{blue}\textrm{rule}} \: : \: {\color{blue}\textrm{base set}} \big\}
$$

 

where the ${\color{blue}\textrm{rule}}$ is an expression (or formula) that depends on a variable that *constructs* elements of our set when the variable runs over some ${\color{blue}\textrm{base set}}.$ 

For example, the set $A,$ given by

$$
A = \big\{ 2n+1\, : \, n\in\mathbb N_0 \big \}
$$

is defined constructively and contains all positive odd numbers:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={2n+1\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}} \\  & ={2(0)+1,\,2(1)+1,\,2(2)+1,\,2(3)+1,\,…} \\  & ={1,3,5,7,…}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Sometimes, it's helpful to write a set using a constructive definition. For example, how might we express the following set constructively?

$$
B = \big\{ 4, 7, 10, 13, \ldots \big\}
$$

First, notice that the elements of our set 

$$
4,\quad 7,\quad 10,\quad 13,\quad \ldots
$$

form an arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=3{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =3 \\  & =7-4 \\  & =10-7 \\  & =13-10 \\  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term $a_n$ of our sequence for $n\in\mathbb N$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\cdot d \\  & =4+(n-1)\cdot 3 \\  & =4+3n-3 \\  & =3n+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set constructively as follows:

$$
B = \big\{ 3n+1 \: : \: n \in \mathbb{N} \big\}
$$

The expression $3n+1$ generates the elements of our set when $n$ runs over $\mathbb{N}.$ 

Note the following:

- A bar "$\mid$" is just as acceptable as a colon to separate the rule from the base set. So, we could also express our set as follows:

$$
B=\big\{ 3n+1 \: \mid \: n \in \mathbb{N} \big\}
$$

- The constructive definition of a given set is typically not unique. For example, we could also define $B$ as follows:

$$
B=\big\{ 3n+4 \: :\: n \in \mathbb{N}_0 \big\}
$$

Notice that we used $\mathbb N_0$ as the base set.

This definition does indeed generate all elements of $B{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{3n+4\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}} & ={3(0)+4,\,3(1)+4,\,3(2)+4,\,3(3)+4,\,…} \\  & ={4,\,7,\,10,\,13,\,…} \\  & =B.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "57358da7-7aa7-5201-b3bd-e43581b18a41" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8307 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "95633ec2-0a87-53d4-9845-589ad5e2c472" :step/math-academy-id 67909 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199426}} {:db/id 17592186199577 :tutorial/content "As previously seen, we can define sets using so-called *constructive definitions* of the form
